Purim. Celebrated on the fourteenth of Adar, falling in February or March, this holiday commemorates the deliverance of Jews from persecution in ancient Persia. Based on the Book of Esther, Purim celebrates the thwarting of Haman's plot to exterminate the Jewish population. It is the most festive and lighthearted of Jewish holidays, marked by costumes, feasting, and playful reversals of social norms.

The Megillah, the Book of Esther, is read aloud twice—once in the evening and once in the morning—with the congregation booing and drowning out Haman's name each time it is mentioned. Costumes and masks are worn, making Purim visually distinctive and playful, with the reversal of identities reflecting Esther's hidden identity as a Jew. Hamantaschen, triangular pastries filled with poppy seeds or jam, are traditional treats, with their three-cornered shape said to represent Haman's hat.

The four mitzvot, or obligations, include sending gifts of food to friends, giving gifts to the poor, feasting, and reading the Megillah. Unlike most Jewish holidays, Purim involves alcohol and intoxication as part of the celebration, seen as a way to express joy and reverse the usual order of things.

The story centers on Queen Esther, a Jewish woman who concealed her identity and became queen of Persia, then risked her life to save her people. Purim is observed even on different dates in different communities; in Jerusalem it is observed on the fifteenth of Adar, known as Shushan Purim. The holiday emphasizes hashgacha, divine providence, with God's presence in the story, though God's name is never mentioned in the Book of Esther. It celebrates Jewish survival and identity through a narrative of hidden redemption.
